readings.title: An Encounter — part 1: doors of escape
readings.challenge: Separate the adventure the narrator imagines from the day he actually has.
readings.focus: Escape through stories, and the gap between romance and an ordinary day.
readings.context: From Joyce’s Dubliners (1914), fifteen stories of Dublin life around 1900. A boy at a Catholic college tells of playing truant. The Union Jack, Pluck and The Halfpenny Marvel were cheap boys’ papers; miching means playing truant; National School boys attended the free state schools; the Pigeon House was a fort and power station at the mouth of the river Liffey. A bob is a shilling and a tanner sixpence. “Swaddlers” was a slang term for Protestants.
readings.contentNote: The boys’ games imitate Wild West stereotypes of Native Americans, and the narrator refers to a fellow passenger as “a little Jew with a bag”; these belong to the story’s world and period.

excerpt.locator: An Encounter, from the opening through the abandoned walk to the Pigeon House; opens “It was Joe Dillon who introduced the Wild West to us. He had a little library made up of…”; closes “…in behind some clouds and left us to our jaded thoughts and the crumbs of our provisions.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the narrator join the Wild West games, and what does he say the stories gave him?
facilitatorNotes: He is one of the “reluctant Indians,” afraid of seeming studious or weak. The adventures are remote from his nature, but they “opened doors of escape.” He wants a way out more than he wants the stories themselves.
evidence: the reluctant Indians who were afraid to seem studious or lacking in robustness, I was one
they opened doors of escape

questions.prompt: What does Father Butler’s rebuke reveal about the school’s values beyond disapproval of cheap reading?
facilitatorNotes: He contrasts “boys like you, educated” with National School boys, so the offence is partly against class standing. The rebuke still awakens “one of my consciences” in the narrator: he notices Leo Dillon’s confused face.
evidence: I could understand it if you were . . . National School boys.
the confused puffy face of Leo Dillon awakened one of my consciences

questions.prompt: How does the day measure up to the narrator’s idea that real adventures “must be sought abroad”?
facilitatorNotes: They see ships and foreign sailors and imagine geography taking substance, but they never reach the Pigeon House, and the day ends with tiredness and crumbs. His search for green-eyed sailors is a private notion he cannot explain. The romance keeps shrinking into the ordinary.
evidence: real adventures, I reflected, do not happen to people who remain at home: they must be sought abroad
left us to our jaded thoughts and the crumbs of our provisions

readings.title: An Encounter — part 2: the man in the field
readings.challenge: Infer what the narrator does not name from what he notices and avoids looking at.
readings.focus: An adult’s menace felt through repetition, and a boy’s shame at his own pride.
readings.context: Recap: the narrator and Mahony have played truant, wandered the docks and Ringsend, and given up on reaching the Pigeon House. They rest in a field. A josser is an old fellow; Thomas Moore, Walter Scott and Lord Lytton were popular nineteenth-century writers.
readings.contentNote: A stranger’s predatory talk with two boys, an implied act of indecency and a fixation on whipping; nothing explicit is described.

excerpt.locator: An Encounter, from the old man’s approach to the end of the story; opens “There was nobody but ourselves in the field. When we had lain on the bank for some time…”; closes “…to bring me aid. And I was penitent; for in my heart I had always despised him a little.”.

questions.prompt: How does the narrator’s wish to seem bookish shape his first response to the man?
facilitatorNotes: He pretends to have read every book mentioned and is pained when Mahony asks a naive question, afraid the man will think him as stupid as Mahony. His vanity draws him into the man’s confidence and separates him from his friend.
evidence: I pretended that I had read every book he mentioned
I was afraid the man would think I was as stupid as Mahony

questions.prompt: How does Joyce convey the man’s disturbance without describing his actions directly?
facilitatorNotes: Through the narrator’s impressions of repetition and circling speech, and through Mahony’s exclamation, which the narrator neither answers nor looks up at. The story gives the effect of the man’s mind and leaves the act unnamed.
evidence: his mind was slowly circling round and round in the same orbit
As I neither answered nor raised my eyes

questions.prompt: The narrator once looked for sailors with green eyes. What is the effect of meeting “bottle-green eyes” here?
facilitatorNotes: The adventure he imagined arrives in a frightening form: the strange figure he half sought is a menacing adult. The echo links romantic longing to danger and turns the day’s quest back on him.
evidence: I met the gaze of a pair of bottle-green eyes peering at me from under a twitching forehead

questions.prompt: Why is the narrator “penitent” at the end?
facilitatorNotes: He is ashamed of his “paltry stratagem” of false names and of his forced bravery, and he recognizes that Mahony, whom he secretly despised, runs to him as if to help. The encounter exposes his own pride as well as the man’s menace.
evidence: I was ashamed of my paltry stratagem
And I was penitent; for in my heart I had always despised him a little.

readings.title: After the Race
readings.challenge: Hear how the narration borrows Jimmy’s excitement while letting the reader see more than he does.
readings.focus: Money, nationality and a young man’s wish to belong among the wealthy.
readings.context: From Joyce’s Dubliners (1914), fifteen stories of Dublin life around 1900. In 1903 the Gordon Bennett Cup, an international motor race, was run in Ireland. Jimmy Doyle, son of a rich Dublin butcher, rides home with Continental friends. Kingstown is a harbour town south of Dublin; Cadet Roussel is a French song; an I.O.U. is a written promise to pay.

excerpt.locator: After the Race; complete individual work; opens “The cars came scudding in towards Dublin, running evenly like pellets in the groove of…”; closes “"Daybreak, gentlemen!"”.

questions.prompt: What does the opening paragraph suggest about the Irish spectators and the visiting cars?
facilitatorNotes: The wealth and industry of the Continent speed through “this channel of poverty and inaction,” and the crowd cheers like the “gratefully oppressed.” The irony frames Irish onlookers as admirers of power they do not share.
evidence: through this channel of poverty and inaction the Continent sped its wealth and industry
the cheer of the gratefully oppressed

questions.prompt: How do Jimmy’s father’s history and Jimmy’s knowledge of money raise the stakes of the evening?
facilitatorNotes: The father modified his Nationalist views, made money through shops and police contracts, and is now a “merchant prince.” Jimmy knows how hard the money was got together, yet he is about to stake most of it to belong among Ségouin’s set.
evidence: His father, who had begun life as an advanced Nationalist, had modified his views early.
knew well with what difficulty it had been got together

questions.prompt: How do sentences like “It must have been a good speech” reveal the limits of Jimmy’s understanding?
facilitatorNotes: The narration takes on his excited, uncertain point of view; he is unsure what he said, who is winning, or even which cards he holds. The exclamations sound like his enthusiasm while showing that he is being carried along.
evidence: It must have been a good speech.
Jimmy did not know exactly who was winning but he knew that he was losing.

questions.prompt: Who wins the last game and who loses, and why might the ending be read politically?
facilitatorNotes: The game lies between Routh, the Englishman, and Ségouin, the Frenchman; Jimmy and the American Farley lose most. Villona, the poor Hungarian who did not play, announces daybreak. Some readers see Ireland’s position among richer nations; others read a simpler moral of a young man’s folly. Both can use the closing details.
evidence: Jimmy understood that the game lay between Routh and Ségouin.
glad of the dark stupor that would cover up his folly

readings.title: Two Gallants — part 1: a walk and a plan
readings.challenge: Work out an unstated plan from what two men say and avoid saying.
readings.focus: Flattery, dependence and the treatment of a young woman as a resource.
readings.context: From Joyce’s Dubliners (1914), fifteen stories of Dublin life around 1900. Two men in their late twenties walk through Dublin on a Sunday evening. A gallant is a fashionable man attentive to women; a slavey is a servant girl; racing tissues are betting tips; a Lothario is a seducer; “on the turf” here means working as a prostitute.
readings.contentNote: Crude slang about women, the sexual and financial exploitation of a young servant, and a woman said to have turned to prostitution.

excerpt.locator: Two Gallants, from the opening through the walk to Kildare Street; opens “The grey warm evening of August had descended upon the city and a mild warm air, a memory…”; closes “"She's a fine decent tart," he said, with appreciation; "that's what she is."”.

questions.prompt: How does the description of Lenehan undercut the youthful image his clothes present?
facilitatorNotes: Breeches, white shoes and a jaunty waterproof “expressed youth,” but his waist, scant grey hair and ravaged face tell a different story. He is acting a part he has outgrown.
evidence: His breeches, his white rubber shoes and his jauntily slung waterproof expressed youth.
had a ravaged look

questions.prompt: What has Corley received from the young woman so far, and what does he hide from her?
facilitatorNotes: She brings him cigarettes, pays his tram fare and once gave him two cigars from her employer. He has hidden his name and lied about his job. The relationship is already one in which he takes.
evidence: Cigarettes every night she'd bring me and paying the tram out and back.
She doesn't know my name.

questions.prompt: Why does Lenehan leave his flattery “open to the interpretation of raillery”?
facilitatorNotes: He depends on Corley and must please him, but mocking undertones let him keep some self-respect. Corley, not subtle, takes the praise straight. The sentence shows a parasite managing his own servility.
evidence: A shade of mockery relieved the servility of his manner.
To save himself he had the habit of leaving his flattery open to the interpretation of raillery.

readings.title: Two Gallants — part 2: the gold coin
readings.challenge: Follow Lenehan alone for most of the evening and read what the final gesture reveals.
readings.focus: Loneliness, appetite and the meaning of a small gold coin.
readings.context: Recap: Lenehan, a hanger-on, walks with Corley, who boasts of a servant girl who gives him gifts and believes he is respectable; Lenehan anxiously asks whether Corley can “pull it off.” The harp is an emblem of Ireland, and “Silent, O Moyle” is a Thomas Moore song of a king’s daughter turned into a swan. “A little of the ready” means some ready money.
readings.contentNote: Implied sexual and financial exploitation of a young servant woman.

excerpt.locator: Two Gallants, from the harpist in Kildare Street to the end of the story; opens “They walked along Nassau Street and then turned into Kildare Street. Not far from the…”; closes “…opened it slowly to the gaze of his disciple. A small gold coin shone in the palm.”.

questions.prompt: How might the harpist and his harp comment on the young woman and on Ireland?
facilitatorNotes: The harp is weary of strangers’ eyes and her master’s hands, her covering fallen about her knees. The image of a used, exposed instrument anticipates the servant girl and suggests a nation played upon by others.
evidence: His harp, too, heedless that her coverings had fallen about her knees, seemed weary alike of the eyes of strangers and of her master's hands.

questions.prompt: What does Lenehan long for in the refreshment bar, and how does the way he imagines it limit the longing?
facilitatorNotes: He wants a home, a warm fire and a good dinner; he feels his “poverty of purse and spirit.” Yet he imagines getting it through a “simple-minded girl” with money, repeating Corley’s calculation in a gentler key.
evidence: This vision made him feel keenly his own poverty of purse and spirit.
if he could only come across some good simple-minded girl with a little of the ready

questions.prompt: Why does the story withhold what Corley wanted until the last sentence, and what does “disciple” suggest?
facilitatorNotes: The reader, like Lenehan, assumes a sexual conquest; the coin reveals that the aim was money, probably taken from her employer. “Disciple” turns Lenehan into a follower before a mock revelation. The title’s “gallants” becomes bitterly ironic.
evidence: opened it slowly to the gaze of his disciple
A small gold coin shone in the palm.

readings.title: Counterparts — part 1: the copy and the retort
readings.challenge: Track the pressures that build in Farrington across an afternoon at work.
readings.focus: Humiliation, thirst and a moment of wit that changes nothing.
readings.context: From Joyce’s Dubliners (1914), fifteen stories of Dublin life around 1900. Farrington is a copying clerk in a solicitors’ office, writing out legal documents by hand. A g.p. is a glass of plain porter; a curate here is a barman; a snug is a small private room in a pub; an order on the cashier is an advance on wages.
readings.contentNote: Workplace bullying and drinking; a client is described as “of Jewish appearance,” a dated stereotype in the narration.

excerpt.locator: Counterparts, from the opening through Mr. Alleyne’s threat after the retort; opens “The bell rang furiously and, when Miss Parker went to the tube, a furious voice called…”; closes “…quit the office instanter! You'll quit this, I'm telling you, or you'll apologise to me!"”.

questions.prompt: How do the bodies of Farrington and Mr. Alleyne set up their conflict?
facilitatorNotes: Farrington is tall, heavy and wine-faced; Alleyne is a little man with an egg-like, hairless head. Farrington stares at the “polished skull,” “gauging its fragility”: physical strength confronts social power.
evidence: The man stared fixedly at the polished skull which directed the affairs of Crosbie & Alleyne, gauging its fragility.

questions.prompt: What does the unfinished legal sentence show about Farrington’s afternoon?
facilitatorNotes: He stares at “In no case shall the said Bernard Bodley be . . .,” notices the alliteration, and finally writes “Bernard Bernard.” His work stalls on a formula of prohibition while his thirst and rage take over.
evidence: thought how strange it was that the last three words began with the same letter
he wrote Bernard Bernard instead of Bernard Bodley and had to begin again on a clean sheet

questions.prompt: Is the retort a triumph or a disaster for Farrington?
facilitatorNotes: It is a brilliant answer to a trap question, found “almost before he was aware of it,” and it astonishes even its author. But it gives Alleyne grounds to demand an apology or dismissal. The wit wins the moment and loses the position.
evidence: almost before he was aware of it, his tongue had found a felicitous moment
You'll apologise to me for your impertinence or you'll quit the office instanter!

readings.title: Counterparts — part 2: rounds and a beating
readings.challenge: Follow the evening’s gains and losses and see how the last scene repeats the first.
readings.focus: Humiliation passed down from master to clerk to child.
readings.context: Recap: Farrington, a clerk who drinks, failed to finish a copy, was berated by his employer Mr. Alleyne, and answered him with a cutting retort before the whole office. A pawn-office lends money against goods; a crown is five shillings; a half-one and small hot specials are whiskeys; Apollinaris is mineral water; the Tivoli was a music hall.
readings.contentNote: Heavy drinking and sexual leering; the story ends with a father beating his young son with a stick.

excerpt.locator: Counterparts, from the section break after the office scene to the end of the story; opens “******”; closes “…say a Hail Mary for you, pa, if you don't beat me. . . . I'll say a Hail Mary. . . ."”.

questions.prompt: How does the retort change as Farrington prepares and tells it?
facilitatorNotes: He composes the narration in advance, adding coolness and timing (“taking my time, you know”) and a slightly altered wording. Higgins later performs it too. The retort becomes a pub story whose value lies in the telling.
evidence: As he walked on he preconsidered the terms in which he would narrate the incident to the boys:
Then I looked back at him again—taking my time, you know.

questions.prompt: Why is it ironic that Farrington hates “a sponge”?
facilitatorNotes: He has pawned his watch and stood rounds to win admiration, and he has thought of borrowing from Pat and Higgins. Resenting Weathers for accepting drinks shows his generosity was a purchase of status. The line exposes his self-deception.
evidence: If there was one thing that he hated it was a sponge.

questions.prompt: How does the arm-wrestling match repeat the office scene?
facilitatorNotes: Called on to uphold the national honour, he is beaten twice by a “stripling,” as earlier a small man mastered him by rank. His fury again finds no proper target and turns on the barman.
evidence: Farrington's dark wine-coloured face flushed darker still with anger and humiliation at having been defeated by such a stripling.
What the hell do you know about it?

questions.prompt: What does the title “Counterparts” mean once you reach the last scene?
facilitatorNotes: A counterpart is a duplicate copy of a legal document, Farrington’s trade, and also a person who mirrors another. He mimics his son’s accent as he once mimicked Alleyne’s, and bullies the weaker as he was bullied; his wife and he bully each other in turn. The boy’s offer of a Hail Mary is a plea for mercy that the story leaves unanswered.
evidence: He began to mimic his son's flat accent
I'll say a Hail Mary for you, pa, if you don't beat me.
